output:
La Chaux-de-Fonds, 1 January 1900, before dawn

Monsieur l'Inspecteur,

I am writing while the house is still quiet. You will come back within the hour, and I would rather you had this from me than from the clocks.

I told you that I went out at a quarter to eleven by my watch, after the repeater would have sounded. That was not true. I rose from the card table before the repeater sounded, and I went up to the atelier while Odile was playing. I asked her to play so that the piano would cover my steps on the stairs. She did, and she never knew why.

Aurèle was at his bench under the long windows with the repeater in his hand. He had been waiting, he said, to show me the slide. I struck him once from behind with the mallet from his own bench. I will not describe the rest.

He fell, and as he fell he pressed the slide. The repeater struck ten low notes, then two doubled, then eight high. I counted them. I could not have stopped myself. Anyone in this town counts a repeater, and I have counted every watch I have ever heard. Ten, and thirty-eight minutes past. The room was full of that sound, and then it was not.

I then stopped the regulator's pendulum and moved its hands back to five past ten, an hour when I had sat at cards with Odile in full view. It was a clumsy thing to do. I have since thought that a man who has just heard a repeater should not expect a room to be quiet afterwards.

I came down, took my cigars from my coat in the hall, and was back in the salon before the hall clock struck its eleven. Odile stopped playing when I came in. I hope you will not press her on that. She was only listening for me.

You will have found the reason already. In 1889 I attended Jules Monnier in his last illness. I gave him laudanum, and on a bad night I gave him too much. I signed the certificate as heart failure, and for ten years nobody asked me otherwise. Aurèle found his brother's last letter among the papers he was sorting for the new century. He did not ask me to explain it. He told me in the hall, before dinner, that he would tell Félix at midnight and the authorities after. He said he would settle his accounts at the turn of the century. He meant it, and I find I mean it too.

Félix did not kill his uncle, and neither did Lina, nor Girard, nor Rosa. Whatever they heard or saw, they heard and saw it without knowing what it meant. Please see that they are told nothing they have not earned.

My own watch was fast all evening. I had not thought to correct it, and I did not think of it as a witness. I see now that I should have.

Tempus edax rerum. Aurèle would have liked that tag, and he would have been right about the watch.

Casimir Vauthier
